title: Deep_Well
description: An ancient well, dated to the early 6th millennium BCE (5900 BCE), found submerged 10m below current sea level. It was a cylindrical shaft 1.5m in diameter and 5.7m deep, dug through clay and into kurkar. A second well was found 100m north, dug into clay and lined with stone. | Hebrew: עתלית ים | Region: Coastal Plain | Era: 01. Paleolithic & Epi-Paleolithic (-20000 to -10000 BCE) | Section: 2.2.1 | Pages: 43, 44

title: Deep_Well
description: A well found at a Halafian culture site (5200 BCE), considered by Campbell to be the oldest well in the world. Most of its upper part was destroyed during the excavation of an irrigation channel. | Hebrew: ח'רבת ג'אראסור | Region: Syria | Era: 01. Paleolithic & Epi-Paleolithic (-20000 to -10000 BCE) | Section: 2.2.2 | Pages: 44

title: Water_Reservoir
description: A complex water system including artificial channels (two long, two short) leading to 'wells' (interpreted as reservoirs/basins) in a shallow depression. This system was designed to collect and store runoff water from a catchment area of about 29 dunams, potentially holding up to 13,900 cubic meters. A settlement located on the eastern outskirts of Amman, Jordan, near a spring. | Hebrew: עין ע'זאל / אבן אל-ע'אזי | Region: Jordan | Era: 02. Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) (-8300 to -5500 BCE) | Section: 2.2.3, 2.2 | Pages: 45, 46, 48

title: Deep_Well
description: A well, approximately 6 meters deep, demonstrating advanced hydrological and engineering knowledge, construction capabilities, and quarrying skills of the inhabitants. Another well at the site was only partially excavated. | Hebrew: עתלית ים | Region: Coastal Plain | Era: 02. Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) (-8300 to -5500 BCE) | Section: 2.2 | Pages: 45, 48

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: A settlement where travertine deposits near Bir Abu Rujha and along a sandstone cliff indicate the presence of a now-dry spring that supplied water. The site's location in a valley allowed for rainwater collection and channeling to create moist soil conditions, and water cisterns might also have been used. | Hebrew: ביידא | Region: Jordan | Era: 02. Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) (-8300 to -5500 BCE) | Section: 2.2.6 | Pages: 47, 48

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: A settlement established in clear proximity to the stable and abundant Einan springs, which remain significant water sources today. | Hebrew: בייסמון | Region: Upper Galilee | Era: 02. Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) (-8300 to -5500 BCE) | Section: 2.2 | Pages: 46

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: A prehistoric settlement where travertine deposits up to 3 meters thick indicate the presence of an ancient spring, now dry, which served as the water source for the community. | Hebrew: גלגל 1 | Region: Jordan Valley | Era: 02. Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) (-8300 to -5500 BCE) | Section: 2.2 | Pages: 46, 47

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: A settlement from the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A period, located near the Elisha Spring in the Jordan Valley. | Hebrew: יריחו | Region: Jordan Valley | Era: 02. Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) (-8300 to -5500 BCE) | Section: 2.2 | Pages: 46

title: Deep_Well
description: A well, briefly reported from Northern Iraq, without detailed information, dimensions, or drawings. Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) (-8300 to -5500 BCE) | Section: 2.2 | Pages: 45

title: Water_Reservoir
description: A settlement established near a freshwater lake (Lake Salibiya), which formed as the Lisan Lake receded, indicating a wetter climate than today. | Hebrew: נתיב הגדוד | Region: Jordan Valley | Era: 02. Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) (-8300 to -5500 BCE) | Section: 2.2.5 | Pages: 47, 48

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: A settlement located near the Ein Yiftah'el spring in the Lower Galilee. | Hebrew: יפתחאל | Region: Lower Galilee | Era: 02. Pre-Pottery Neolithic (PPN) (-8300 to -5500 BCE) | Section: 2.2 | Pages: 46

title: Deep_Well
description: Two wells were found. One from layer VI (5750-5600 BCE) is a circular, stone-lined well, 3.2m deep, with a diameter of 1.5m at the top, narrowing to 1.25m at the bottom. The second from layer II (5400-5250 BCE) is a rectangular, stone-lined well located in a courtyard within a fortress. Both had evidence of water drawing mechanisms. | Hebrew: הצ'ילר (תורכיה) | Region: Turkey | Era: 03. Pottery Neolithic (PN) (-5500 to -4500 BCE) | Section: 2.3.2 | Pages: 50

title: Deep_Well
description: Five circular pits were found, one of which was excavated to 0.7m depth, dug into hard clay and lined with kurkar and limestone. It had an outer diameter of 1.5m and an inner diameter of 0.8-0.9m, identified as a well. | Hebrew: כפר גלים צפון | Region: Coastal Plain | Era: 03. Pottery Neolithic (PN) (-5500 to -4500 BCE) | Section: 2.3.1.ב | Pages: 49

title: Deep_Well
description: A rectangular pit (1x0.8m) dug to 2m depth, constructed with alternating layers of stone and oak wood, widening at the bottom. It is identified as a well, unique in its construction method, and possibly used for capturing fresh water springs. | Hebrew: כפר סמיר | Region: Coastal Plain | Era: 03. Pottery Neolithic (PN) (-5500 to -4500 BCE) | Section: 2.3.1.א | Pages: 49, 51

title: Deep_Well
description: Three pits were found, one of which was partially excavated to 0.4m depth. These pits are considered potential wells or water collection points, possibly for capturing fresh water springs. | Hebrew: מגדים | Region: Coastal Plain | Era: 03. Pottery Neolithic (PN) (-5500 to -4500 BCE) | Section: 2.3.1.ג | Pages: 49

title: Deep_Well
description: A bottle-shaped well, 5m deep, dug into virgin soil at the base of the tel, dating to the Halafian culture (6th millennium BCE). It had an oval opening (1.5x1.2m) and a maximum diameter of 3.1m in the middle, with pottery showing signs of prolonged water exposure. | Hebrew: טפה גאורה | Region: Iraq | Era: 03. Pottery Neolithic (PN) (-5500 to -4500 BCE) | Section: 2.3.3 | Pages: 50

title: Deep_Well
description: A round well, 1.5-1.55m in inner diameter and 2.45m deep, constructed of dry-laid fieldstones. It was dug into gravel alluvium next to a wadi channel and was associated with a building and courtyard. | Hebrew: אבו חוף | Region: Shephelah | Era: 04. Chalcolithic Period (-4500 to -3300 BCE) | Section: 2.4.1 | Pages: 52, 54

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: A Chalcolithic temple complex demonstrating a strong connection to the natural springs in its vicinity. The proximity to these springs suggests their cultic significance and use during this period. | Hebrew: עין גדי | Region: Judean Hills | Era: 04. Chalcolithic Period (-4500 to -3300 BCE) | Section: 2.4 Summary | Pages: 54

title: Deep_Well
description: A cylindrical well, 2m in diameter and 3m deep, excavated into loess soil down to the ancient streambed of Nahal Beersheba. Two steps were cut into its upper walls, and it was intentionally filled at a later stage. | Hebrew: חורבת בתר | Region: Negev | Era: 04. Chalcolithic Period (-4500 to -3300 BCE) | Section: 2.4.2 | Pages: 52, 54

title: Deep_Well
description: An abandoned well, located about 1 km west of the megalithic complex, characterized by small stones, troughs, and rope marks. Its Chalcolithic dating is suggested but not definitively confirmed without excavation. | Hebrew: ראג'אג'יל (ערב הסעודית) | Region: Saudi Arabia | Era: 04. Chalcolithic Period (-4500 to -3300 BCE) | Section: 2.4.4 | Pages: 53, 54

title: Deep_Well
description: An Ubaid period well, 1.15m in diameter at its rim, excavated to a depth of 12-13m. It was found a few centimeters below the holy of holies floor of the northern temple of Layer XIII, and its water was used by the city's acropolis. | Hebrew: טפה גאורה | Region: Mesopotamia | Era: 04. Chalcolithic Period (-4500 to -3300 BCE) | Section: 2.4.3 | Pages: 53, 54

title: Water_Reservoir
description: A large open-air reservoir in Area K, exceeding 1800 cubic meters in volume, 25m wide, and 2.5m deep. It was designed to collect runoff water from the upper city via channels, featuring a stone floor on clay and a thick dam wall, dating to EB 1-3. The only known instance of plaster from this period is from a water pool at Ai, where impermeable clayey soil was used as a hydraulic material to line the reservoir. | Hebrew: העי (א-תל) | Region: Judean Hills | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.10, 2.5 | Pages: 59, 71

title: Deep_Well
description: The site shows evidence of rainwater storage in soft chalk bedrock, indicating the use of rock-cut cisterns during the Early Bronze Age. | Hebrew: ברקת | Region: Shephelah | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5 | Pages: 68

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: A permanent spring in the Western Negev Highlands, serving as a crucial water source around which Early Bronze Age settlements were concentrated. | Hebrew: עין קדיס | Region: Negev | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.9 | Pages: 59

title: Water_Reservoir
description: Three water collection systems and two modified natural pools (P3, P4) with a total capacity of 1800 cubic meters. The system involved diverting water from Wadi Rajil with a diversion dam and channels to fill the pools, dated to the Early Bronze Age. | Hebrew: ג'ווה | Region: Jordan | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.12 | Pages: 65, 66

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: A permanent spring in the Western Negev Highlands, serving as a crucial water source around which Early Bronze Age settlements were concentrated. | Hebrew: קדש ברנע (עין אל-קודייראת) | Region: Negev | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.9 | Pages: 59

title: Water_Tunnel_Shaft
description: Three stepped shafts were excavated, leading to a groundwater level approximately 60m deep. One shaft is 100m long, reaching the bottom of Wadi Shallala. Horizontal tunnels and connecting stepped tunnels were proposed to bring water into the city, dated to EB 2-3. | Hebrew: חירבת זירקון | Region: Jordan | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.3 | Pages: 56, 57

title: Deep_Well
description: Multiple rock-cut cisterns, including a large one (B3) 5m deep and another (D7) with niches, were used for rainwater collection via rock-cut channels. These cisterns were unplastered due to the impermeable Nari and chalk bedrock. | Hebrew: מצר | Region: Coastal Plain | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.15 | Pages: 68

title: Deep_Well
description: This Early Bronze Age settlement, like others in Western Samaria, utilized unplastered cisterns carved into soft chalk bedrock to collect rainwater, compensating for the absence of nearby springs. | Hebrew: מידיא | Region: Samaria | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.14 | Pages: 67, 68

title: Deep_Well
description: A well near Mount Ramon, possibly originating in the Early Bronze Age (or even Pre-Pottery Neolithic) when the water table was higher, despite its later Ottoman reconstruction. | Hebrew: נחל חורשה עילי (באר) | Region: Negev | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.9 | Pages: 59

title: Deep_Well
description: Four wells were discovered, cut into a water-bearing layer. One well, well-preserved, has a 1.5-1m opening, is bell-shaped, 1.5m deep, and lined with stones. Its dating to the Chalcolithic and Early Bronze Age is based on nearby flint tools. Two methods of water storage were identified: 'granot' (runoff collection basins), dams, and depressions in clay, in addition to wells. These systems were associated with Early Bronze Age 2 settlement clusters. | Hebrew: בקעת עובדה | Region: Negev | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.1, 2.5.13 | Pages: 55, 66

title: Deep_Well
description: This Early Bronze Age settlement, located near a spring, also featured unplastered cisterns carved into soft chalk bedrock for rainwater collection, a common practice in Western Samaria. | Hebrew: שבתין | Region: Samaria | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.14 | Pages: 67, 68

title: Deep_Well
description: A well is located in the heart of the Early Bronze Age city. Although re-used in the Iron Age, it is suggested that its initial excavation dates to the Early Bronze Age as part of a larger runoff water collection system. An open-air pool/reservoir in the city center, formed by collecting rainwater runoff through radial streets into a natural depression, covering about one dunam. Water collection from rooftops into large pithoi is also suggested for this EB city. Arad had central water pools for collecting runoff, and large storage jars (pithoi) were used within houses for water storage. Clayey soil was used as a hydraulic plaster for water installations. | Hebrew: תל ערד | Region: Negev | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.2, 2.5.11, 2.5 | Pages: 55, 56, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 70, 71

title: Aqueduct_Channel
description: A basalt-lined tunnel, roofed with basalt slabs, was discovered on the southern edge of Tel Bet Yerah. It is interpreted as part of an Early Bronze Age III water system, possibly an aqueduct bringing water from mountain springs or a channel collecting runoff within the city. | Hebrew: בית ירח | Region: Jordan Valley | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.17 | Pages: 70

title: Deep_Well
description: A fortified Early Bronze Age settlement with several rock-cut cisterns in soft chalk bedrock, designed to collect rainwater. One examined cistern was irregular, 2.2m deep to the chamber, with a rectangular chamber 2.6x2.0m, showing no signs of plaster due to the impermeable chalk. Shallow wells in nearby wadis likely supplemented water supply during peacetime. | Hebrew: תל דלית | Region: Judean Hills | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.16 | Pages: 68, 69, 70

title: Ancient_City_Water_System
description: Despite massive city walls, an Early Bronze Age water system was likely present, possibly a depression in the northern part of the tel, though specific details are scarce due to later archaeological layers. | Hebrew: תל מגידו | Region: Jezreel Valley | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5 | Pages: 71

title: Deep_Well
description: This Early Bronze Age settlement, like others in Western Samaria, utilized unplastered cisterns carved into soft chalk bedrock to collect rainwater, compensating for the absence of nearby springs. | Hebrew: תל מצפון לפחמה | Region: Samaria | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.14 | Pages: 67, 68

title: Deep_Well
description: This Early Bronze Age settlement, like others in Western Samaria, utilized unplastered cisterns carved into soft chalk bedrock to collect rainwater, compensating for the absence of nearby springs. | Hebrew: תל ליד בזריה | Region: Samaria | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.14 | Pages: 67, 68

title: Water_Reservoir
description: Although no formal water system has been discovered for the Early Bronze Age, a clear topographical depression at the lowest point of the 150-dunam city likely served to collect runoff water. | Hebrew: תל ירמות | Region: Shephelah | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5 | Pages: 71

title: Deep_Well
description: Two wells were found. The older well (Layer VIIIb, Late Uruk/EB) was 2.8m in diameter, excavated to 24m, plastered with mud, and featured steps, connected to a bitumen-lined drainage channel. A second well (Layer VI, early 3rd millennium BCE) also had a drainage channel leading to it. | Hebrew: טפה גאורה | Region: Mesopotamia | Era: 05. Early Bronze Age (EB) (-3300 to -2200 BCE) | Section: 2.5.4 | Pages: 57

title: Deep_Well
description: A well in the northern part of the tel, dated to the Middle Bronze Age, which was abandoned along with a house and garden it supplied with water. | Hebrew: בוצרה (סוריה) | Region: Syria | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.13 | Pages: 89

title: Deep_Well
description: A very deep well in the lower city, connecting to a dome-roofed underground chamber, containing artifacts dated to around 2000 BCE. | Hebrew: אבלה (סוריה) | Region: Syria | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.12 | Pages: 88, 89

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: During the Middle Bronze Age, the city of Jericho was fortified, and Elisha's Spring (Ein es-Sultan) was intentionally included within its city walls to provide a secure water source. | Hebrew: יריחו | Region: Jordan Valley | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.3 | Pages: 75

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: The Gihon Spring was the primary water source for Jerusalem from the Chalcolithic period, and its abundant flow was seven times greater than the city's needs during the Middle Bronze Age. Channel I, a plastered channel partly cut into rock and partly built, is considered the oldest water system in the area, possibly dating to the Middle Bronze Age or earlier, used for irrigating agricultural plots in the Kidron Valley. The central water system of Jerusalem, including Warren's Shaft (tunnel part), the Great Tower, a pool, and Channels II and III, was carved and built during Middle Bronze Age II to provide the city with an internal water source, especially during sieges. | Hebrew: ירושלים (עיר דוד) | Region: Judean Hills | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.4 | Pages: 76, 77, 78, 79, 80, 81

title: Aqueduct_Channel
description: Textual evidence from King Yahdun-Lim (18th century BCE) describes the construction of canals to bring water to Mari, potentially representing an early urban aqueduct, though no archaeological evidence has been found. | Hebrew: מארי | Region: Mesopotamia | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.25 | Pages: 94

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: During Middle Bronze Age II, a spring was enclosed within the walls of the kingdom city of Qatna, while a stream outside the rampart may have filled a moat for defense. | Hebrew: קטנה | Region: Syria | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.5 | Pages: 81

title: Plastered_Cistern
description: A burial cave from MB IIB was originally a rock-cut, mud-plastered water cistern, approximately 3m deep and 3m in diameter, with spiral steps for access. | Hebrew: שעלבים | Region: Shephelah | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.22 | Pages: 92

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: The city of Dan, enclosed by a massive rampart, incorporated the eastern springs of Dan within its fortifications during the Middle Bronze Age, serving as the primary water source. An artificial water passage (sinkhole) was likely constructed concurrently with the rampart to manage excess water. | Hebrew: תל דן | Region: Upper Galilee | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.2 | Pages: 73, 74, 75

title: Water_Tunnel_Shaft
description: A water system consisting of an elliptical vertical shaft with steps, cut into the kurkar rock, was constructed during Middle Bronze Age IIA within the fortified city of Tel Gerisa to reach groundwater, likely for use during sieges. | Hebrew: תל גריסה | Region: Coastal Plain | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.6 | Pages: 82, 83

title: Water_Tunnel_Shaft
description: An impressive water system was discovered within the fortifications of Tel Gezer, comprising an entrance, a sloping tunnel with steps, a collection basin, and a cave, dating to the Middle Bronze Age. A large, complex stepped water tunnel, 40m long and nearly 40m deep, leading to a natural spring/groundwater source. The author argues for its construction in the Middle Bronze Age. Numerous bottle-shaped, rock-cut, and often plastered cisterns were found, typically 4.9-7m deep, with drainage channels collecting runoff. Specific examples like 23089 and 34046 are dated to the Middle Bronze Age, with some reused into later periods. | Hebrew: תל גזר | Region: Shephelah | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.7, 2.6.23 | Pages: 83, 84, 85, 86, 93, 94

title: Deep_Well
description: A 2m diameter, 11.5m deep well, lined with kurkar stones and rock-cut, located within the Middle Bronze Age city, intended to supply water during sieges. Dated by MB II pottery. | Hebrew: תל הרור | Region: Northern Negev | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.11 | Pages: 88

title: Water_Tunnel_Shaft
description: A large depression in the lower city is suggested to be the top of a shaft dug to groundwater, used during the Middle Bronze and Late Bronze Ages. Six bottle-shaped, rock-cut cisterns (e.g., 9024, 9027, 6243) were found, dated to MB II by pottery, with some continuing into LB. They featured narrow necks, expanding bodies, and sometimes plaster, designed to collect rainwater runoff. | Hebrew: תל חצור | Region: Upper Galilee | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.8, 2.6.21 | Pages: 87, 91, 92

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: A large planned city from MB II (c. 1800 BCE) was built around the abundant Ein Shefa spring, which was enclosed within the city's rampart. Excess water was likely drained through a channel in the western gate. | Hebrew: תל כברי | Region: Western Galilee | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.1 | Pages: 73

title: Deep_Well
description: A 44m deep, 2.4m diameter cylindrical well, stone-lined and rock-cut, located within the city's Middle Bronze Age fortifications and used until the Iron Age. | Hebrew: תל לכיש | Region: Shephelah | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.10 | Pages: 88

title: Water_Tunnel_Shaft
description: A large depression in the northern part of the tel is hypothesized to be an early water system (MB, LB, possibly EB) reaching groundwater, potentially connected to Ein el-Qubi. | Hebrew: תל מגידו | Region: Jezreel Valley | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.8 | Pages: 87

title: Deep_Well
description: An unfortified settlement featured a rectangular/oval well, 2.3m deep, lined with fieldstones, dated to MB IIA. Its bottom is 1.2m below current sea level, indicating a lower sea level in the MB period. | Hebrew: תל נאמי | Region: Coastal Plain | Era: 06. Middle Bronze Age (MB) (-2200 to -1550 BCE) | Section: 2.6.9 | Pages: 87

title: Spring_Cave_Capture
description: A cave leading to an underground corridor with a spring at its base, accessed by eight flights of stairs from the Acropolis. The entrance was sealed during sieges. Pottery dates the end of its use to the second half of the 13th century BCE. | Hebrew: אתונה (יוון) | Region: Greece | Era: 07. Late Bronze Age (LB) (-1550 to -1200 BCE) | Section: 2.7.3.a | Pages: 99

title: Water_Tunnel_Shaft
description: A deep water shaft, 52m deep, with a staircase descending along its side, dug to reach groundwater. The excavation was documented in two texts and took 100 days with 120 workers. The bottom was moist, suggesting groundwater was reached. | Hebrew: מצר | Region: Sinai / Egypt | Era: 07. Late Bronze Age (LB) (-1550 to -1200 BCE) | Section: 2.7.4 | Pages: 100, 101

title: Ancient_City_Water_System
description: An underground system with hidden clay pipes transporting water from the Perseia spring (360m away) to an internal reservoir within the city walls, accessed by a stepped passage. Dated to the 13th century BCE. Additionally, two wells were found within the city walls, and two external springs served settlements outside the walls. | Hebrew: מיקנה (יוון) | Region: Greece | Era: 07. Late Bronze Age (LB) (-1550 to -1200 BCE) | Section: 2.7.3.b | Pages: 99, 100

title: Water_Reservoir
description: A plastered pool (4162) measuring 3.2x1.5m, found in Area G within a governor's house or palace (Strata XIV-XVII, Late Bronze Age II). It had two phases, with a brick layer beneath the plaster floor, and a drainage channel leading to a stone-lined drainage pit. Water likely collected from roofs or was manually brought from a well. | Hebrew: תל אשדוד | Region: Coastal Plain | Era: 07. Late Bronze Age (LB) (-1550 to -1200 BCE) | Section: 2.7.8 | Pages: 103, 104

title: Plastered_Cistern
description: Numerous rock-cut, plastered cisterns (at least 24) were found, dating to Stratum IV (Late Bronze Age). They had narrow necks built up with fieldstones and a sump at the bottom. The widespread use of plaster is highlighted. | Hebrew: תל בית שמש | Region: Shephelah | Era: 07. Late Bronze Age (LB) (-1550 to -1200 BCE) | Section: 2.7.7 | Pages: 103

title: Deep_Well
description: A deep well, 13m deep and 0.86m in diameter, found in the southeastern part of Tel Beit She'an. Its walls were built of bricks for 11.9m, with the rest being earlier fill. Dated to Stratum IXa (14th century BCE). | Hebrew: תל בית שאן | Region: Jordan Valley | Era: 07. Late Bronze Age (LB) (-1550 to -1200 BCE) | Section: 2.7.1 | Pages: 98

title: Deep_Well
description: A sealed well, evidenced by large stones with rope marks and a depression that fills with water, located 400m southwest of Nahal Besor, at the foot of the acropolis. Possibly dates to the initial phase of the lower city in the Late Bronze Age. | Hebrew: תל ג'מה | Region: Negev | Era: 07. Late Bronze Age (LB) (-1550 to -1200 BCE) | Section: 2.7.2 | Pages: 98

title: Water_Reservoir
description: A large underground water reservoir (No. 357) in the Upper City, within the Late Bronze Age palace area (Stratum XIV). It features a built entrance corridor with a corbelled arch and a rock-cut section extending 30m to a depth of 8.5m, ending in a cruciform shape. It was plastered and had carved steps, with a capacity of about 150 cubic meters. Initially, it might have been a burial cave (Stratum XV) before being converted to a reservoir. A bottle-shaped cistern, dated to the Late Bronze Age, found in the western part of the Iron Age water system entrance. Its neck was destroyed during the Iron Age construction, but it contained many intact Late Bronze Age vessels. | Hebrew: תל חצור | Region: Upper Galilee | Era: 07. Late Bronze Age (LB) (-1550 to -1200 BCE) | Section: 2.7.5 | Pages: 101, 102

title: Water_Reservoir
description: A square shaft (1.45m side, 7.4m preserved height) initially intended as a stepped well to groundwater, but excavation was halted. The entire system, including the shaft, was plastered to serve as a reservoir. Dated to Late Bronze Age I, possibly after Thutmose III's campaign (1468 BCE). | Hebrew: תל תענך | Region: Jezreel Valley | Era: 07. description: Hezekiah's Tunnel, a 533m long rock-cut channel, diverted water from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam within the city walls, constructed in the late 8th century BCE (late Iron Age II) during King Hezekiah's reign. A large pool (15x15m during the First Temple period) located at the southern end of Hezekiah's Tunnel, serving as the primary reservoir for the diverted Gihon Spring waters within the city. Hezekiah's Tunnel, a 530m long rock-cut tunnel, was constructed in the 8th century BCE (Iron II) to divert water from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam inside the city walls, a complex engineering feat involving two teams digging from opposite ends. Warren's Shaft, a natural vertical karstic shaft (13m deep), was accidentally discovered in the 8th century BCE during preparations for Hezekiah's Tunnel, leading to attempts to connect it to the Gihon Spring and integrate it into the water system. Channel IV, an overflow channel originating near the Pool of Siloam and extending to the Kidron Valley, is considered by some scholars to be an original part of Hezekiah's Tunnel, dating its construction to the 8th century BCE. Various pools mentioned in biblical texts (e.g., Upper Pool, Lower Pool, Old Pool, Pool of Siloam) likely collected runoff water, serving as secondary water sources for the city, primarily for non-drinking uses during the Iron Age. The 'Hasmonean Water Channel,' a rock-cut channel near the Temple Mount, collected runoff water for cisterns. Although named Hasmonean, some scholars propose it dates to the First Temple period (Iron Age). Bir Ayub, identified with biblical Ein Rogel, is a 38m deep well fed by a small cave and fissures. Its water was primarily used for irrigating fields and gardens, and its biblical mentions indicate its use during the Iron Age. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. An aqueduct system within the city, likely feeding a reservoir or pool, was present in Jerusalem during the Iron Age II. title: Water_Tunnel_Shaft
description: The Eupalinos Tunnel, built in the 6th century BCE, is a 1040m long tunnel cut through a mountain to supply water from a spring to the city of Samos. It included an initial 890m covered aqueduct section, vertical shafts, and a complex rock-cut tunnel with a deep trench for water pipes, demonstrating advanced engineering. An aqueduct bringing water from a distance outside the city was found at Samos, dating to the Iron Age II. | Hebrew: מנהרת אופלינוס (סמוס) | Region: Greece | Era: 09. Iron Age II (-1000 to -586 BCE) | Section: 2.9.48 | Pages: 182, 183, 191

title: Ancient_City_Water_System
description: A water system for the fortress, including a deep well (25.19m deep, 4.6m diameter) outside the walls, and a covered rock-cut channel (24m long) leading under the city wall to three large plastered cisterns (approx. 250 cubic meters) inside the fortress. The system collected runoff and was supplemented by water from the well. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. Wells were found at Tel Arad, which are dated with high probability to the Iron Age II period. A reservoir with an external feeding system was identified at Tel Arad during the Iron Age II. | Hebrew: תל ערד | Region: Negev | Era: 09. title: Water_Reservoir
description: A monumental, cruciform-shaped rock-cut reservoir (24x23.5m, 6m high) in Area C, fed by multiple channels collecting runoff, was constructed in the 10th century BCE (Iron IIA) and reused in the 7th century BCE. A round cistern in Area B, dated to Iron Age II, measuring 5.75m in diameter and 7m deep. It features a 0.6m diameter opening, a 5m neck (3m built, 2m rock-cut), and 10cm thick gray plaster. Its estimated volume is 87 cubic meters. A rock-cut, spherical cistern in Area A, dated to Iron Age II, with a 1x1m square opening and a 1.5m neck, reaching a depth of 4.5m. Its volume is approximately 15 cubic meters (excluding the neck), with traces of disintegrated plaster found. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, specifically mentioning a cruciform-shaped reservoir designed to maximize storage volume and prevent roof collapse. A reservoir or pool was found at Tel Beit Shemesh, dated to the Iron Age II period. title: Water_Tunnel_Shaft
description: Megiddo features a complex water system with two main phases. The 'gallery' (secret passage) providing access to a natural cave and well is dated by Yadin to the 10th century BCE (Iron Age IIA). A later, monumental system, also from Iron Age II, includes a large shaft (36m deep) and a 50m long tunnel, constructed to access the same water source from within the city walls. Megiddo's impressive water system, consisting of a pit and a tunnel, is attributed by the author and most scholars to Iron Age II. A plastered reservoir with a monumental staircase, located outside the outer gate (Locus 2153), was supplied by the nearby Ein Kubi spring or collected runoff. It is dated to the time of Ahab (Iron II). Mentioned as a site with an underground water system where a pulley could have been used, similar to the one depicted in an Assyrian relief, suggesting a sophisticated water supply during sieges. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with three monumental water systems, likely involving tunnels or shafts to access groundwater within the fortified city. A major water system, cut to a spring or groundwater within the fortified city, was found at Tel Megiddo, dating to the Iron Age II. A reservoir with an external feeding system was identified at Tel Megiddo during the Iron Age II. | Hebrew: תל מגידו | Region: Jezreel Valley | Era: 09.
